source: Authored by hand against data/manifest.json. Chapter coverage was read off the mirrored PDFs in data/ncert-original/. Not generated — see data/prerequisites.schema.md.

prerequisites.why: Real Numbers restarts exactly where Class 9 stopped: rationals, irrationals, and why some decimals stop and others repeat.
recap: Every real number is either rational (a fraction p/q with q not 0) or irrational (√2, π — no fraction gives it).
A rational number's decimal either terminates or repeats. It terminates only when the denominator, in lowest terms, is made of 2s and 5s.
√2 is irrational by contradiction: assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms, and you can always show p and q are both even. Class 10 reuses that argument unchanged.

prerequisites.why: Half of this chapter is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic applied to HCF and LCM, and that arithmetic is built in Class 6-8.
You have already met polynomials in one variable and drawn their graphs. Class 10 only raises the degree.
recap: A linear polynomial is ax + b with a not 0. Its graph is a straight line.
Its zero is the x where the value is 0 — where the line crosses the x-axis. Solve ax + b = 0 to get x = -b/a.
"Zero of a polynomial" and "x-intercept of its graph" are the same fact said twice.

prerequisites.why: Finding the zeroes of a quadratic means factorising it, which is the algebra-tiles work from Class 9.
recap: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b², (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b².
To factorise x² + px + q, find two numbers that add to p and multiply to q.

prerequisites.why: A pair of linear equations is a pair of straight lines, and the solution is where they cross.
recap: A linear relationship plots as a straight line: pick two values of x, get two points, join them.
Two lines that cross once give one solution; parallel lines give none; the same line twice gives infinitely many.

prerequisites.why: The graphical method is plotting, so placing and reading points has to be automatic before the method is worth anything.
recap: A point is (x, y): x steps along from the origin, y steps up.
Signs pick the quadrant. (-, +) is top-left, (-, -) is bottom-left.

prerequisites.why: A quadratic equation is a quadratic polynomial set equal to zero, so its roots are that polynomial's zeroes under another name.
recap: For ax² + bx + c, the sum of the zeroes is -b/a and the product is c/a.
A quadratic has at most two zeroes — which is why a quadratic equation has at most two roots.

prerequisites.why: The factorisation method is splitting the middle term, and that is Class 9 identity work.
recap: Split the middle term: for x² + 7x + 12, find two numbers adding to 7 and multiplying to 12 — 3 and 4.
Then x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4), and a product is zero only when one bracket is zero.

prerequisites.why: Completing the square is one identity run backwards. If (a + b)² is not automatic, the method looks like a trick instead of a step.
recap: (x + k)² = x² + 2kx + k². Read it right to left: given x² + 2kx, the missing piece is k².
So x² + 6x becomes (x + 3)² - 9: halve the 6, square it, add it, take it away again.
That is the whole method. The quadratic formula is this done once with letters instead of numbers.

prerequisites.why: Class 9 already builds arithmetic progressions and the sum of the first n terms. Class 10 formalises the same two rules.
recap: A sequence follows a rule. In an AP the rule is: add the same number every time. That number is the common difference d.
Explicit rule: the nth term is a + (n - 1)d. Recursive rule: each term is the one before it plus d.
Sum of the first n terms: pair the first with the last. S = n/2 × [2a + (n - 1)d].

prerequisites.topic: Congruence of triangles, and ratio and proportion
prerequisites.why: Similarity is congruence with the equal-sides condition relaxed to equal ratios. Without congruence criteria and comfortable ratio work, the AA and SSS similarity rules have nothing to stand on.
prerequisites.note: The Class 9 NCF Mathematics book (Ganita Manjari) carries no triangles chapter, so this genuinely has no earlier chapter in this app.

prerequisites.why: The coordinate plane and the distance formula are both Class 9. Class 10 adds one new formula on top of them.
recap: Plot (x, y): x along, y up. The origin is (0, 0).
Distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is √[(x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²] — Pythagoras on the gap in x and the gap in y.
The only genuinely new thing in Class 10 is the section formula, for a point cutting a segment in a given ratio.

prerequisites.why: Sin, cos and tan only exist because similar right triangles have identical side ratios. That is the similarity chapter, two chapters back.
recap: Two triangles are similar when their angles match; then their matching sides are all in the same ratio.
So in any right triangle with a given acute angle, opposite/hypotenuse is a fixed number whatever the size. That number is the sine of the angle.
Pythagoras, a² + b² = c², is what turns one known ratio into the other two.

prerequisites.why: A height-and-distance question is one right triangle and one ratio. If the ratios are shaky the diagram will not save you.
recap: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent.
Know 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° by heart. Almost every question in this chapter uses nothing else.
Angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal; angle of depression is measured down from it.

prerequisites.why: Class 9 defines the circle, its chords and the angles they subtend. Class 10 adds exactly one object to that picture: the tangent.
recap: A circle is every point at the same distance — the radius — from the centre.
A chord joins two points on the circle. A chord through the centre is a diameter.
A tangent touches at exactly one point, and it is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point. Almost every Class 10 proof starts there.

prerequisites.why: Arc length and sector area are already in the Class 9 perimeter-and-area chapter. Class 10 mostly combines them with a triangle.
recap: Circumference = 2πr. Area = πr².
An arc is a fraction of the circumference: (θ/360) × 2πr. A sector is the same fraction of the area: (θ/360) × πr².
A segment is the sector minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.

prerequisites.why: Every surface-area formula here is a flat area wrapped around a solid, so the flat areas have to be solid first.
recap: Rectangle = l × b. Triangle = ½ × base × height. Circle = πr².
The curved surface of a cylinder is a rectangle rolled up: 2πr × h.

prerequisites.topic: Volume and surface area of cubes, cuboids and cylinders
prerequisites.why: Class 10 combines solids — a cone on a hemisphere, a cylinder with a cone scooped out. The single solids themselves are Class 8.
prerequisites.note: The Class 9 NCF Mathematics book covers plane figures only, so the solids are nowhere in this app.

prerequisites.topic: Mean, median, mode and reading a frequency table
prerequisites.why: Class 10 Statistics is these three averages recomputed for grouped data. The ungrouped versions are Class 7-8.
prerequisites.note: The Class 9 NCF Mathematics book has no statistics chapter, so there is no earlier chapter in this app to send you to.

prerequisites.why: Class 9 introduces probability from first principles. Class 10 uses the same definition on harder sample spaces.
recap: P(event) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes.
It always lands between 0 and 1, and P(not E) = 1 - P(E).
Write the sample space out first. Two dice give 36 outcomes, not 12 — that one slip costs more marks here than anything else.

prerequisites.why: Writing an equation needs chemical formulae, and balancing one is the law of conservation of mass. Both are Class 9, chapter 9.
recap: Mass is conserved: every atom on the left must appear on the right. That is the only reason equations are balanced at all.
A formula comes from valency, criss-crossed: calcium (2+) with chlorine (1-) gives CaCl2.
(s), (l), (g) and (aq) mark the state. (aq) means dissolved in water.

prerequisites.why: Valency decides every formula you will write this year, and valency comes from where the electrons sit.
recap: Electrons fill shells 2, 8, 8. Valency is how many an atom must gain, lose or share to fill its outer shell.
Sodium has one spare electron, so valency 1. Oxygen is two short, so valency 2.

prerequisites.why: Balancing is not a puzzle with a trick. It is the law of conservation of mass, and the law is what tells you which numbers you are allowed to change.
recap: Atoms are neither made nor destroyed in a reaction, so the count of each element must match on both sides.
Change only the coefficient in front of a formula. Changing a subscript makes it a different substance, not a balanced one.
Count one element at a time, leave hydrogen and oxygen until last, then check every element once more.

prerequisites.why: Neutralisation, and every acid test in this chapter, is a reaction you have to write and balance first.
recap: Acid + base gives salt + water. Metal + acid gives salt + hydrogen.
Balance by counting atoms of each element on both sides. Never rewrite a formula to make it balance.

prerequisites.why: pH and dilution are statements about concentration, which is the Class 9 solutions chapter.
recap: Concentration is how much solute sits in how much solution.
Diluting adds water. The amount of solute does not change, so the concentration falls.
That is why acid is added to water and never water to acid — the heat needs somewhere to go.

prerequisites.why: Ionic bonding — a metal handing electrons to a non-metal — is the single idea that explains how metals behave.
recap: A metal loses electrons and becomes a positive ion. A non-metal gains them and becomes negative.
The two attract, and that is the ionic bond: high melting point, brittle, conducts only when molten or dissolved.

prerequisites.why: The reactivity series is read straight off displacement reactions, so you have to recognise one on sight.
recap: In a displacement reaction a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound.
Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons. Reduction is the opposite. Both happen in the same reaction.

prerequisites.why: Every structure you draw this chapter is a covalent bond diagram, which Class 9 already taught.
recap: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Neither atom loses one outright.
Carbon has 4 outer electrons and shares all 4 — which is why every carbon in a correct structure shows exactly four bonds.

prerequisites.why: Catenation and the homologous series are counting arguments about valency. Get valency wrong and every formula after it is wrong.
recap: Valency is the number of bonds an atom forms: carbon 4, hydrogen 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3.
That is why the alkane series steps up by CH2 each time — one more carbon needs two more hydrogens to stay full.

prerequisites.why: Nutrition, respiration and transport happen inside a cell before they happen inside you.
recap: The cell is the unit of life. The membrane decides what gets in and what leaves.
Mitochondria release energy; chloroplasts capture light. Respiration and photosynthesis are things organelles do.

prerequisites.why: Transport in plants is two tissues and nothing else, and you met both last year.
recap: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job.
Xylem carries water and minerals up. Phloem carries food in both directions.

prerequisites.why: A reflex arc is nervous tissue wired to muscular tissue. Both were named and drawn in Class 9.
recap: Nervous tissue is made of neurons: dendrites take the signal in, the axon carries it out.
Muscular tissue contracts, which is how a signal becomes a movement.
A reflex is that pair wired through the spinal cord — the brain is told afterwards rather than asked first.

prerequisites.why: Class 9 already sets out why organisms reproduce and what variation is for. Class 10 fills in the organs.
recap: Asexual reproduction makes copies from one parent. Sexual reproduction mixes DNA from two.
The mixing is the point: variation is what lets a species survive a change in its surroundings.
Cell division is the mechanism underneath both.

prerequisites.why: Mendel's rules only make sense once gametes do. Everything in Heredity rests on one set of chromosomes coming from each parent.
recap: Gametes carry one set of chromosomes each. Fertilisation puts two sets back together.
So you hold two copies of every gene, one from each parent — that is what a pair like Tt means.
Sex determination in humans is the same fact: the egg always gives X, the sperm gives X or Y.

prerequisites.why: Class 10 opens with the laws of reflection already assumed and moves straight to curved mirrors. If plane mirrors are shaky, the sign convention will not stick.
prerequisites.note: The Class 9 NCF Science book (Exploration) has no light chapter, so this app holds nothing earlier to open.

prerequisites.why: The eye is one convex lens and one screen. Every defect and every correction in this chapter is the previous chapter's lens formula.
recap: A convex lens converges light to a focus. The eye's lens does exactly this, onto the retina.
1/v - 1/u = 1/f, and power P = 1/f in dioptres. Myopia and hypermetropia corrections are this formula and nothing more.
Refraction bends light when it changes medium. Dispersion is refraction that bends each colour by a different amount.

prerequisites.why: Electrical energy and power are the same work-and-power definitions from Class 9, with charge doing the moving.
recap: Work is force × distance. Energy is the capacity to do work. Both are measured in joules.
Power is work per second, measured in watts. A 60 W bulb converts 60 joules every second.
In Class 10 this becomes W = VIt and P = VI. Same definitions, electrical quantities.

prerequisites.topic: Electric current, cells and circuit diagrams
prerequisites.why: Ohm's law arrives on page one assuming you can already read a circuit diagram and say what a cell does.
prerequisites.note: The Class 9 NCF Science book has no electricity chapter, so there is no earlier chapter here to open.

prerequisites.why: Every magnetic effect in this chapter starts from a current. No current, no field — so the previous chapter has to be solid.
recap: Current is charge per second, and it only flows round a closed loop.
Ohm's law V = IR fixes how much current a given voltage drives through a given resistance.
A bigger current gives a stronger field. That one sentence answers most of the field-pattern questions here.

prerequisites.why: Class 9 already treats the Earth as one system, with energy flowing through it and matter cycling round. Class 10 narrows that to the ecosystem.
recap: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat. It flows one way and does not come back.
Matter does come back: the water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles are the same atoms reused.
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next, which is why food chains are short.

prerequisites.why: F = ma says a force produces acceleration. If acceleration is still vague, the law is just three letters.
recap: Speed is distance per second. Velocity is speed with a direction attached.
Acceleration is change of velocity per second — so turning at a steady speed is still acceleration.
On a distance-time graph the slope is speed. On a velocity-time graph the slope is acceleration and the area is distance.

prerequisites.why: Work is defined in terms of force and displacement, so the force chapter has to come first.
recap: A force changes motion. With no net force, motion does not change at all.
Work is done only when a force moves its point of application along the direction of the force.
No displacement, or a force at right angles to the motion, means zero work — however tired you are.

prerequisites.why: Bonding and formulae are decided by the outer shell, so the structure of the atom has to be settled first.
recap: An atom is a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around it.
Atomic number = number of protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons.
Electrons fill 2, then 8, then 8. The outer shell alone decides how the atom combines.

prerequisites.why: Identities are statements about polynomials, so the vocabulary — term, degree, like terms — has to be in place.
recap: A polynomial is a sum of terms like 3x² - 5x + 2. Its degree is the highest power.
Like terms have the same variable to the same power. Only like terms can be added.

prerequisites.why: Half this chapter measures circles, using the names the circles chapter has just defined.
recap: The radius runs centre to edge; the diameter is twice it.
An arc is a piece of the circle's edge. A sector is the slice between two radii.

prerequisites.topic: Data handling: tallies, tables and simple chance
prerequisites.why: Probability starts by counting outcomes in a table. The counting, not the probability, is where most of the marks go.
prerequisites.note: This is the first probability chapter in the corpus, so there is nothing earlier here to open.
